901.quote_or_event: “In this world, I have seen love to be false. Whether they are spouses or friends, all are concerned only with their own happiness.”
901.explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur warns that attachment (moh) to spouse and friends cannot be life's goal, since worldly ties are bound up with self-interest and do not lead to God.
901.tie_back: The Kural says that doting on a wife costs a man life's highest fruit; Gurbani agrees that attachment can pull one from the highest aim, but it applies this to every worldly tie and to both partners.
901.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 536, Raag Dayv Gandhaaree, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
901._accuracy_note: Next-best: Gurbani warns against moh in general and does not single out a husband's devotion to his wife; Sikhism honours marriage and does not share the chapter's view of women.

902.quote_or_event: “O sexual desire, you lead the mortals to hell; you make them wander in reincarnation through countless species.”
902.explanation: Guru Arjan addresses kaam (lust), one of the five thieves, as a force that drags people away from their true purpose.
902.tie_back: The Kural says the man who drops his duties out of desire for his wife brings shame on himself, and Gurbani likewise treats being ruled by desire as a downfall.
902.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1358, Salok Sehskritee, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
902._accuracy_note: Next-best: shares the warning against being ruled by desire, but the verse concerns lust in general, not married love, and does not frame the problem as yielding to a wife.

903.quote_or_event: “So why call her bad? From her, kings are born.”
903.explanation: Guru Nanak rejects the low view of women common in his time, pointing out that every person, kings included, is born of woman.
903.tie_back: The Kural calls a husband's deference to his wife unnatural and shameful; Guru Nanak's verse offers a counterpoint, refusing to treat women as inferior.
903.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 473, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
903._accuracy_note: Contrast rather than parallel: Sikh teaching affirms women's dignity and does not regard respect for a wife as shameful, so it disagrees with this kural's assumption.

904.quote_or_event: “While laughing, playing, dressing and eating, he is liberated.”
904.explanation: Guru Arjan teaches that liberation is reached within ordinary household life, by one who has met the True Guru, not by leaving it.
904.tie_back: The Kural fears that a man ruled by his wife fails as a householder and loses the merit of the next world; Sikhism agrees the household is where one earns spiritual reward, though it does not make the wife the threat.
904.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 522, Raag Gujri (Gujri ki Vaar), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
904._accuracy_note: Partial and indirect: it backs the Kural's high regard for householder duty, but says nothing about a husband's fear of his wife.

905.quote_or_event: “One who works for what he eats, and gives some of what he has”
905.explanation: Guru Nanak describes the true way as honest work (kirat karni) and sharing its fruits with others (vand chhakna).
905.tie_back: The Kural regrets a man too afraid of his wife to give from his own earnings to the deserving; for Sikhs, sharing what one honestly earns is a basic duty.
905.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Saarang (Vaar), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
905._accuracy_note: Next-best: it matches the duty of giving from one's own earnings, but nothing in it concerns domestic fear or blames the wife.

906.quote_or_event: “They are not said to be husband and wife, who merely sit together. They alone are called husband and wife, who have one light in two bodies.”
906.explanation: Guru Amar Das defines true marriage as a spiritual partnership of two people sharing one divine light, not a relationship of domination or fear.
906.tie_back: The Kural mocks men who live in fear of their wives; Gurbani replaces that picture of rule and fear with partnership between equals.
906.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 788, Raag Soohee (Vaar), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
906._accuracy_note: Contrast more than parallel: both care about a healthy marriage, but Sikhism's ideal of spiritual equality does not fit the Kural's ranking of husband over wife.

907.quote_or_event: Mai Bhago (Mata Bhag Kaur) openly rebuked forty Sikhs who had deserted Guru Gobind Singh during the siege of Anandpur; shamed, they followed her back, and they fought beside her at Khidrana (Muktsar) in 1705, where the Guru honoured the fallen as the Chali Mukte, the Forty Liberated Ones.
907.explanation: A woman's courage and sense of honour exposed and then redeemed the failure of men who had abandoned their duty.
907.tie_back: The Kural says a modest woman's dignity is worth more than the so-called manhood of a man who has lost his own; Mai Bhago's story shows a woman's honour shaming and restoring men who had faltered.
907.source: Wikipedia, 'Mai Bhago' (drawing on the Oxford Encyclopedia of Women in World History and other works)
907._accuracy_note: Partial: it supports a woman's honour outshining men who lost their nerve, but the Kural's target is a man ruled by his wife, not deserters; Wikipedia was used as a last resort, and some details of her life are traditional.

908.quote_or_event: “In the midst of this world, do seva, and you shall be given a place of honor in the Court of the Lord.”
908.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that selfless service in ordinary life is what earns honour before God.
908.tie_back: The Kural says a man who lives only to please his wife neither helps his friends nor does good deeds; Gurbani calls everyone to active service of others.
908.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 26, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
908._accuracy_note: Next-best: it shares the call to do good for others, but says nothing about being led by a spouse; the Sikh duty of seva falls equally on women and men.

909.quote_or_event: “The four cardinal blessings are obtained by serving the Lord.”
909.explanation: Guru Arjan says the four traditional aims of life (dharma, wealth, desire and liberation) come through devotion to God.
909.tie_back: The Kural says virtue, wealth and pleasure all slip away from a man who obeys his wife in everything; Gurbani names the same aims but says they are secured by right devotion.
909.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 108, Raag Maajh, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
909._accuracy_note: Partial: it shares the framework of life's aims, which matches the Kural's aram, porul and inbam, but it gives the positive source of those aims rather than warning about domestic subservience.

910.quote_or_event: “See the brotherhood of all mankind as the highest order of Yogis; conquer your own mind, and conquer the world.”
910.explanation: In Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak teaches that mastering one's own mind is the real victory.
910.tie_back: The Kural says a mind given to careful thought will never be wholly ruled by attachment, and Japji likewise makes self-mastery the foundation of every other success.
910.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 6, Japji Sahib (Pauri 28), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
910._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on a disciplined mind not being ruled by attachment; Japji is about mastering the self in general and does not cast women as the danger.
